stem_en: What is the form of government of the United States?
explanation_en: The United States is a republic: the people hold the power and exercise it through elected representatives, under a written Constitution that limits what government may do. USCIS also accepts “constitution-based federal republic” and “representative democracy.”

stem_en: What is the supreme law of the land?
explanation_en: The Constitution, written in 1787, is the supreme law of the land. Every other law, federal or state, must agree with it, and the Supreme Court can strike down laws that do not.

stem_en: Name one thing the U.S. Constitution does.
options_en: Sets the national budget each year
acceptable_en: Protects the rights of the people
explanation_en: The Constitution sets up the government, defines its powers and its parts (the three branches), and protects the rights of the people. Any one of those is a full answer.

stem_en: The U.S. Constitution starts with the words “We the People.” What does “We the People” mean?
options_en: The states are supreme over the nation
explanation_en: “We the People” means the government’s power comes from the people themselves: popular sovereignty, consent of the governed, self-government. The Constitution opens with these words to say who is in charge.

stem_en: How are changes made to the U.S. Constitution?
options_en: By a simple majority vote in Congress
explanation_en: The Constitution is changed through amendments. Article V sets the process: a proposal by two-thirds of Congress (or a convention), then ratification by three-quarters of the states. It is deliberately hard; only 27 amendments have passed.

stem_en: What does the Bill of Rights protect?
options_en: The right of states to leave the Union
acceptable_en: (The basic) rights of people living in the United States
explanation_en: The Bill of Rights — the first ten amendments, ratified in 1791 — protects the basic rights of Americans and of everyone living in the United States: speech, religion, press, assembly, petition, fair trials and more.

stem_en: How many amendments does the U.S. Constitution have?
explanation_en: There are 27 amendments. The first ten are the Bill of Rights (1791); the most recent, the 27th, took effect in 1992 and concerns congressional pay.

stem_en: Why is the Declaration of Independence important?
options_en: It set the number of states at thirteen forever.
It says America is free from British control.
acceptable_en: It says America is free from British control.
It says all people are created equal.
explanation_en: Adopted July 4, 1776, the Declaration of Independence announced that the colonies were free from British control and declared that all people are created equal, with inherent rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness.

stem_en: What founding document said the American colonies were free from Britain?
explanation_en: The Declaration of Independence, written mainly by Thomas Jefferson and adopted on July 4, 1776, said the thirteen American colonies were free from Britain.

stem_en: Name two important ideas from the Declaration of Independence and the U.S. Constitution.
explanation_en: The founding documents share a set of ideas: equality, liberty, the social contract, natural rights, limited government and self-government. Name any two for the oral test.

stem_en: The words “Life, Liberty, and the pursuit of Happiness” are in what founding document?
explanation_en: “Life, Liberty, and the pursuit of Happiness” are the inherent rights named in the Declaration of Independence (1776), not in the Constitution.

stem_en: What is the economic system of the United States?
explanation_en: The United States has a capitalist, free-market economy: businesses and individuals own property and decide what to make, buy and sell, with prices set by the market rather than by the government.

stem_en: What is the rule of law?
options_en: The president may ignore court rulings.
Judges may make any law they wish.
acceptable_en: No one is above the law.
explanation_en: The rule of law means everyone must follow the law — citizens, leaders and the government itself. No one is above the law, which is what makes power accountable.

stem_en: Many documents influenced the U.S. Constitution. Name one.
explanation_en: The Constitution drew on earlier documents: the Declaration of Independence, the Articles of Confederation, the Federalist and Anti-Federalist Papers, the Virginia Declaration of Rights, the Fundamental Orders of Connecticut, the Mayflower Compact and the Iroquois Great Law of Peace.

stem_en: There are three branches of government. Why?
options_en: Because the Constitution required three founders
So the states can govern themselves
So one part does not become too powerful
acceptable_en: So one part does not become too powerful
explanation_en: Power is split among the legislative, executive and judicial branches so that no one part becomes too powerful. This is separation of powers, enforced through checks and balances: each branch can limit the others.

stem_en: What is the supreme law of the land?
explanation_en: The Constitution, written in 1787, is the supreme law of the land. Every other law, federal or state, must agree with it, and the Supreme Court can strike down laws that do not.

stem_en: What does the Constitution do?
options_en: Sets the national budget each year
explanation_en: The Constitution sets up the government, defines how it works and protects the basic rights of Americans. Any one of those three is a full answer.

stem_en: The idea of self-government is in the first three words of the Constitution. What are these words?
explanation_en: The Constitution begins “We the People.” Those three words place the source of government power with the people — the idea of self-government.

stem_en: What is an amendment?
explanation_en: An amendment is a change or addition to the Constitution. There have been 27; the first ten are the Bill of Rights.

stem_en: What do we call the first ten amendments to the Constitution?
explanation_en: The first ten amendments, ratified in 1791, are called the Bill of Rights. They protect freedoms such as speech, religion, press, assembly and the right to a fair trial.

stem_en: What is one right or freedom from the First Amendment?
options_en: The right to a driver’s license
explanation_en: The First Amendment protects freedom of speech, religion, assembly and the press, and the right to petition the government. Any one of the five is a full answer.

stem_en: How many amendments does the Constitution have?
explanation_en: There are 27 amendments. The first ten are the Bill of Rights (1791); the most recent, the 27th, took effect in 1992.

stem_en: What did the Declaration of Independence do?
options_en: Set up the three branches of government
Gave women the right to vote
acceptable_en: said that the United States is free (from Great Britain)
explanation_en: The Declaration of Independence announced that the United States was free from Great Britain. It was adopted on July 4, 1776.

stem_en: What are two rights in the Declaration of Independence?
explanation_en: The Declaration of Independence names life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness as rights all people hold. Name any two.

stem_en: What is freedom of religion?
options_en: Everyone must belong to a church.
You can practice any religion, or not practice a religion.
The government chooses the national religion.
acceptable_en: You can practice any religion, or not practice a religion.
explanation_en: Freedom of religion means you can practice any religion, or not practice a religion at all. The First Amendment protects it, and it is why the government may not establish an official church.

stem_en: What is the economic system in the United States?
explanation_en: The United States has a capitalist, market economy: private individuals and businesses own property and decide what to make, buy and sell.

stem_en: What is the “rule of law”?
options_en: The president may ignore court rulings.
Judges may make any law they wish.
acceptable_en: No one is above the law.
explanation_en: The rule of law means everyone must follow the law — citizens, leaders and the government itself. No one is above the law, which is what makes power accountable.

stem_en: Name the three branches of government.
explanation_en: The three branches are the legislative (Congress), the executive (the President) and the judicial (the courts). Naming them as Congress, president and the courts is also accepted.

stem_en: The President of the United States is in charge of which branch of government?
explanation_en: The President heads the executive branch, which carries out and enforces the laws. Congress is the legislative branch and the courts are the judicial branch.

stem_en: What part of the federal government writes laws?
explanation_en: Congress — the Senate and the House of Representatives together — is the legislative branch and writes federal laws. The President signs or vetoes them; the courts interpret them.

stem_en: What are the two parts of the U.S. Congress?
options_en: The Cabinet and the Supreme Court
The President and the Vice President
explanation_en: Congress has two chambers: the Senate (100 members, two per state) and the House of Representatives (435 voting members, by population). A bill must pass both to reach the President.

stem_en: Name one power of the U.S. Congress.
explanation_en: Congress writes laws, declares war and makes the federal budget. Only Congress can declare war; the President commands the military once it does.

stem_en: How many U.S. senators are there?
explanation_en: There are 100 senators: two from each of the 50 states, regardless of population. Senators serve six-year terms.

stem_en: How long is a term for a U.S. senator?
explanation_en: A U.S. senator serves a six-year term. Terms are staggered so that about one-third of the Senate is elected every two years.

stem_en: Who is one of your state’s U.S. senators now?
note_en: District of Columbia residents and residents of U.S. territories should answer that D.C. (or the territory where the applicant lives) has no U.S. senators.
explanation_en: Every state elects two U.S. senators for six-year terms. Washington, D.C. and the territories have no senators. The app fills in your state’s current senators from verified Senate records once you set your state.

stem_en: How many voting members are in the House of Representatives?
explanation_en: The House has 435 voting members, a number fixed by law since 1913. Seats are divided among the states by population after each census.

stem_en: How long is a term for a member of the House of Representatives?
explanation_en: Members of the House serve two-year terms, so the whole House faces the voters every even-numbered year.

stem_en: Why do U.S. representatives serve shorter terms than U.S. senators?
options_en: To more closely follow public opinion
Because the House has more members
acceptable_en: To more closely follow public opinion
explanation_en: Representatives serve two years to senators’ six so that they must answer to voters often and follow public opinion closely. The Senate’s longer terms were meant to make it steadier.

stem_en: How many senators does each state have?
explanation_en: Each state has two senators, large or small. That equal representation was the Great Compromise of 1787.

stem_en: Why does each state have two senators?
options_en: Because the president appoints one of them
So the Senate has an even number of members
To match the number of parties
explanation_en: Each state has two senators because of the Great (Connecticut) Compromise of 1787: small states feared being outvoted, so the Senate gives every state equal representation while the House is based on population.

stem_en: Name your U.S. representative.
note_en: Residents of territories with nonvoting Delegates or Resident Commissioners may provide the name of that Delegate or Commissioner. Also acceptable is any statement that the territory has no (voting) representatives in Congress.
explanation_en: Your U.S. representative depends on your congressional district, which the app cannot know from your state alone. Find yours by ZIP code at house.gov and save the name in Settings; residents of D.C. and the territories have a non-voting delegate instead.

stem_en: What is the name of the Speaker of the House of Representatives now?
explanation_en: The Speaker leads the House of Representatives and is second in the line of presidential succession, after the Vice President. The House elects the Speaker at the start of each Congress. The app checks the current holder against speaker.gov.

stem_en: Who does a U.S. senator represent?
explanation_en: A senator represents all the people of their state, not a district within it. A member of the House represents a single congressional district.

stem_en: Who elects U.S. senators?
explanation_en: Senators are elected directly by the citizens of their state. Before the 17th Amendment (1913) state legislatures chose them.

stem_en: Who does a member of the House of Representatives represent?
explanation_en: A member of the House represents the people of one congressional district within a state. Districts are redrawn after each census so they hold roughly equal populations.

stem_en: Who elects members of the House of Representatives?
explanation_en: Citizens of a congressional district elect their representative every two years. Districts, not whole states, are the House’s unit of representation.

stem_en: Some states have more representatives than other states. Why?
options_en: Because they joined the Union earlier
Because they are larger in area
explanation_en: House seats are divided by population: states with more people get more representatives. California has the most; several states have only one.

stem_en: The President of the United States is elected for how many years?
explanation_en: The President is elected to a four-year term. Elections are held every four years in November.

stem_en: The President of the United States can serve only two terms. Why?
options_en: Because Congress sets the limit each year
Because of a Supreme Court ruling
acceptable_en: To keep the president from becoming too powerful
explanation_en: The 22nd Amendment (1951) limits a president to two terms, to keep any one person from becoming too powerful. It was adopted after Franklin Roosevelt won four terms.

stem_en: What is the name of the President of the United States now?
explanation_en: The President is elected to a four-year term and heads the executive branch. The app shows the current President, verified against whitehouse.gov; USCIS accepts the last name alone.

stem_en: What is the name of the Vice President of the United States now?
explanation_en: The Vice President is elected with the President, presides over the Senate and becomes President if the President can no longer serve. The app shows the current Vice President, verified against whitehouse.gov.

stem_en: If the president can no longer serve, who becomes president?
options_en: The Vice President (of the United States)
acceptable_en: The Vice President (of the United States)
explanation_en: If the President can no longer serve, the Vice President becomes President. After the Vice President comes the Speaker of the House.

stem_en: Name one power of the president.
explanation_en: The President signs bills into law or vetoes them, enforces the laws, serves as Commander in Chief of the military and chief diplomat, and appoints federal judges. Any one of these is a full answer.

stem_en: Who is Commander in Chief of the U.S. military?
options_en: The Chairman of the Joint Chiefs
explanation_en: The President is Commander in Chief of the armed forces. Only Congress can declare war, but the President directs the military.

stem_en: Who signs bills to become laws?
explanation_en: After both houses of Congress pass a bill, the President signs it into law — or vetoes it, sending it back to Congress.

stem_en: Who vetoes bills?
explanation_en: The President vetoes bills. Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds vote in both the Senate and the House.

stem_en: Who appoints federal judges?
explanation_en: The President appoints federal judges, including Supreme Court justices, with the advice and consent of the Senate.

stem_en: The executive branch has many parts. Name one.
explanation_en: The executive branch includes the President, the Cabinet and the federal departments and agencies that carry out the laws.

stem_en: What does the President’s Cabinet do?
options_en: Advises the President (of the United States)
acceptable_en: Advises the President (of the United States)
explanation_en: The Cabinet advises the President. It is made up of the Vice President and the heads of the executive departments, such as the Secretary of State and the Attorney General.

stem_en: What are two Cabinet-level positions?
acceptable_en: Secretary of Health and Human Services
Secretary of Housing and Urban Development
Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency
Administrator of the Small Business Administration
Director of the Central Intelligence Agency
Director of the Office of Management and Budget
explanation_en: Cabinet-level positions include the Vice President, the Attorney General and the Secretaries of State, Treasury, War (Defense), the Interior, Agriculture, Commerce, Labor, Health and Human Services, Housing and Urban Development, Transportation, Energy, Education, Veterans Affairs and Homeland Security, plus several agency heads.

stem_en: Why is the Electoral College important?
options_en: It decides who is elected president.
acceptable_en: It decides who is elected president.
It provides a compromise between the popular election of the president and congressional selection.
explanation_en: The Electoral College decides who is elected president. Each state has electors equal to its members of Congress; it was the framers’ compromise between a popular vote and selection by Congress.

stem_en: What is one part of the judicial branch?
explanation_en: The judicial branch is made up of the Supreme Court and the lower federal courts. Judges interpret the law and decide whether laws follow the Constitution.

stem_en: What does the judicial branch do?
acceptable_en: Decides if a law goes against the (U.S.) Constitution
explanation_en: The judicial branch reviews and explains laws, resolves disputes about them, and decides whether a law goes against the Constitution.

stem_en: What is the highest court in the United States?
explanation_en: The Supreme Court is the highest court in the United States. Its decisions are final and bind every other court.

stem_en: How many seats are on the Supreme Court?
explanation_en: The Supreme Court has nine seats: the Chief Justice and eight associate justices. Congress set the number at nine in 1869.

stem_en: How many Supreme Court justices are usually needed to decide a case?
explanation_en: A majority of the nine justices — five — is usually needed to decide a case.

stem_en: How long do Supreme Court justices serve?
explanation_en: Supreme Court justices hold lifetime appointments: they serve until they retire, die or are removed by impeachment.

stem_en: Supreme Court justices serve for life. Why?
options_en: Because judges are hard to replace
To save the cost of elections
explanation_en: Justices serve for life so they can be independent of politics and free from outside pressure: they do not need to please voters or a president to keep their jobs.

stem_en: Who is the Chief Justice of the United States now?
explanation_en: The Chief Justice presides over the Supreme Court and serves for life. The app shows the current Chief Justice, verified against supremecourt.gov; the last name alone is accepted.

stem_en: Name one power that is only for the federal government.
explanation_en: Only the federal government may print paper money, mint coins, declare war, create an army, make treaties and set foreign policy. States may not.

stem_en: Name one power that is only for the states.
explanation_en: The states provide schooling and education, police protection, fire safety, driver’s licenses, and zoning and land-use approval. The federal government does not run these.

stem_en: What is the purpose of the 10th Amendment?
options_en: (It states that the) powers not given to the federal government belong to the states or to the people.
It gives Congress the power to tax income.
It limits the president to two terms.
acceptable_en: (It states that the) powers not given to the federal government belong to the states or to the people.
explanation_en: The 10th Amendment says that powers the Constitution does not give to the federal government belong to the states or to the people. It is the constitutional basis of federalism.

stem_en: Who is the governor of your state now?
note_en: District of Columbia residents should answer that D.C. does not have a governor.
explanation_en: Each state elects its own governor, the head of the state’s executive branch. The app fills in your governor from the National Governors Association roster once you set your state; D.C. has a mayor instead.

stem_en: What is the capital of your state?
note_en: District of Columbia residents should answer that D.C. is not a state and does not have a capital. Residents of U.S. territories should name the capital of the territory.
explanation_en: Every state has a capital city where its legislature meets — often not its largest city. The app fills in your state’s capital once you set your state; D.C. residents answer that D.C. is not a state and has no capital.

stem_en: Name one branch or part of the government.
explanation_en: The three branches are the legislative (Congress), the executive (the President) and the judicial (the courts). Naming any one is a full answer.

stem_en: What stops one branch of government from becoming too powerful?
explanation_en: Checks and balances — the separation of powers among three branches — stop any one branch from becoming too powerful. Each branch can limit the others.

stem_en: Who is in charge of the executive branch?
explanation_en: The President is in charge of the executive branch, which enforces the laws Congress passes.

stem_en: Who makes federal laws?
explanation_en: Congress makes federal laws. It is the national legislature, made up of the Senate and the House of Representatives.

stem_en: What are the two parts of the U.S. Congress?
options_en: The President and the Vice President
The Cabinet and the Supreme Court
explanation_en: Congress has two chambers: the Senate (100 members, two per state) and the House of Representatives (435 voting members, by population). A bill must pass both to reach the President.

stem_en: How many U.S. Senators are there?
explanation_en: There are 100 senators: two from each of the 50 states, regardless of population. Senators serve six-year terms.

stem_en: We elect a U.S. Senator for how many years?
explanation_en: A U.S. senator serves a six-year term; about a third of the Senate is elected every two years.

stem_en: Who is one of your state’s U.S. Senators now?
note_en: District of Columbia residents and residents of U.S. territories should answer that D.C. (or the territory where the applicant lives) has no U.S. Senators.
explanation_en: Every state elects two U.S. senators for six-year terms. Washington, D.C. and the territories have no senators. The app fills in your state’s current senators from verified Senate records once you set your state.

stem_en: The House of Representatives has how many voting members?
explanation_en: The House has 435 voting members, fixed by law since 1913 and divided among the states by population.

stem_en: We elect a U.S. Representative for how many years?
explanation_en: A U.S. representative serves a two-year term, so the whole House is elected every even-numbered year.

stem_en: Name your U.S. Representative.
note_en: Residents of territories with nonvoting Delegates or Resident Commissioners may provide the name of that Delegate or Commissioner. Also acceptable is any statement that the territory has no (voting) Representatives in Congress.
explanation_en: Your U.S. representative depends on your congressional district, which the app cannot know from your state alone. Find yours by ZIP code at house.gov and save the name in Settings; residents of D.C. and the territories have a non-voting delegate instead.

stem_en: Who does a U.S. Senator represent?
explanation_en: A senator represents all the people of their state, not a district within it. A member of the House represents a single congressional district.

stem_en: Why do some states have more Representatives than other states?
options_en: Because they joined the Union earlier
Because they are larger in area
explanation_en: States with more people have more representatives: House seats are divided by population after each census.

stem_en: We elect a President for how many years?
explanation_en: The President is elected for four years and may serve at most two terms.

stem_en: In what month do we vote for President?
explanation_en: Presidential elections are held in November — on the Tuesday after the first Monday — every four years.

stem_en: What is the name of the President of the United States now?
explanation_en: The President is elected to a four-year term and heads the executive branch. The app shows the current President, verified against whitehouse.gov; USCIS accepts the last name alone.

stem_en: What is the name of the Vice President of the United States now?
explanation_en: The Vice President is elected with the President, presides over the Senate and becomes President if the President can no longer serve. The app shows the current Vice President, verified against whitehouse.gov.

stem_en: If the President can no longer serve, who becomes President?
explanation_en: If the President can no longer serve, the Vice President becomes President. After the Vice President comes the Speaker of the House.

stem_en: If both the President and the Vice President can no longer serve, who becomes President?
explanation_en: If both the President and Vice President can no longer serve, the Speaker of the House becomes President, under the Presidential Succession Act.

stem_en: Who is the Commander in Chief of the military?
options_en: The Chairman of the Joint Chiefs
explanation_en: The President is Commander in Chief of the military; only Congress can declare war.

stem_en: Who signs bills to become laws?
explanation_en: After both houses of Congress pass a bill, the President signs it into law — or vetoes it, sending it back to Congress.

stem_en: Who vetoes bills?
explanation_en: The President vetoes bills. Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds vote in both the Senate and the House.

stem_en: What does the President’s Cabinet do?
explanation_en: The Cabinet advises the President. It is made up of the Vice President and the heads of the executive departments, such as the Secretary of State and the Attorney General.

stem_en: What are two Cabinet-level positions?
acceptable_en: Secretary of Health and Human Services
Secretary of Housing and Urban Development
explanation_en: Cabinet-level positions include the Vice President, the Attorney General and the Secretaries of State, Treasury, War (Defense), the Interior, Agriculture, Commerce, Labor, Health and Human Services, Housing and Urban Development, Transportation, Energy, Education, Veterans Affairs and Homeland Security, plus several agency heads.

stem_en: What does the judicial branch do?
acceptable_en: decides if a law goes against the Constitution
explanation_en: The judicial branch reviews and explains laws, resolves disputes about them, and decides whether a law goes against the Constitution.

stem_en: What is the highest court in the United States?
explanation_en: The Supreme Court is the highest court in the United States. Its decisions are final and bind every other court.

stem_en: How many justices are on the Supreme Court?
explanation_en: The Supreme Court has nine seats: the Chief Justice and eight associate justices. Congress sets the number by law; it has been nine since 1869. The app verifies the current count against supremecourt.gov.

stem_en: Who is the Chief Justice of the United States now?
explanation_en: The Chief Justice presides over the Supreme Court and serves for life. The app shows the current Chief Justice, verified against supremecourt.gov; the last name alone is accepted.

stem_en: Under our Constitution, some powers belong to the federal government. What is one power of the federal government?
explanation_en: The federal government alone may print money, declare war, create an army and make treaties. Any one of these is a full answer.

stem_en: Under our Constitution, some powers belong to the states. What is one power of the states?
explanation_en: The states provide schooling, police protection, fire safety and driver’s licenses, and approve zoning and land use.

stem_en: Who is the Governor of your state now?
note_en: District of Columbia residents should answer that D.C. does not have a Governor.
explanation_en: Each state elects its own governor, the head of the state’s executive branch. The app fills in your governor from the National Governors Association roster once you set your state; D.C. has a mayor instead.

stem_en: What is the capital of your state?
note_en: District of Columbia residents should answer that D.C. is not a state and does not have a capital. Residents of U.S. territories should name the capital of the territory.
explanation_en: Every state has a capital city where its legislature meets — often not its largest city. The app fills in your state’s capital once you set your state; D.C. residents answer that D.C. is not a state and has no capital.

stem_en: What are the two major political parties in the United States?
explanation_en: The two major parties are the Democratic Party and the Republican Party. Nearly every member of Congress and every president since the 1850s has belonged to one of them.

stem_en: What is the political party of the President now?
explanation_en: The President’s party is one of the two major parties, Democratic or Republican. The app shows the current President’s party, verified with the officeholder.

stem_en: What is the name of the Speaker of the House of Representatives now?
explanation_en: The Speaker leads the House of Representatives and is second in the line of presidential succession, after the Vice President. The House elects the Speaker at the start of each Congress. The app checks the current holder against speaker.gov.

stem_en: There are four amendments to the U.S. Constitution about who can vote. Describe one of them.
acceptable_en: You don’t have to pay (a poll tax) to vote.
Any citizen can vote. (Women and men can vote.)
A male citizen of any race (can vote).
explanation_en: Four amendments widened the vote: the 15th (1870) — a male citizen of any race can vote; the 19th (1920) — women can vote; the 24th (1964) — no poll tax is needed to vote; the 26th (1971) — citizens 18 and older can vote. Describe any one.

stem_en: Who can vote in federal elections, run for federal office, and serve on a jury in the United States?
options_en: Anyone 18 or older living in the United States
explanation_en: Only U.S. citizens can vote in federal elections, run for federal office and serve on a jury. Permanent residents have many rights, but not these three.

stem_en: What are three rights of everyone living in the United States?
explanation_en: Everyone living in the United States — citizens or not — has freedom of expression, speech, assembly, religion, the freedom to petition the government and the right to bear arms. Name three for the oral test.

stem_en: What do we show loyalty to when we say the Pledge of Allegiance?
explanation_en: The Pledge of Allegiance is a promise of loyalty to the flag and to the United States — “the republic for which it stands.”

stem_en: Name two promises that new citizens make in the Oath of Allegiance.
options_en: Give up loyalty to other countries
Buy a home in the United States
acceptable_en: Give up loyalty to other countries
Obey the laws of the United States
Serve (help, do important work for) the nation (if needed)
Be loyal to the United States
explanation_en: In the Oath of Allegiance new citizens promise to give up loyalty to other countries, defend the Constitution, obey U.S. laws, serve in the military or the nation if needed, and be loyal to the United States. Name any two.

stem_en: How can people become United States citizens?
options_en: Be born in the United States, under the conditions set by the 14th Amendment
Live in the United States for ten years
Own property in the United States
acceptable_en: Be born in the United States, under the conditions set by the 14th Amendment
Derive citizenship (under conditions set by Congress)
explanation_en: People become citizens by birth in the United States under the 14th Amendment, by naturalization, or by deriving citizenship through their parents under conditions set by Congress.

stem_en: What are two examples of civic participation in the United States?
acceptable_en: Give an elected official your opinion (on an issue)
Support or oppose an issue or policy
explanation_en: Civic participation means taking part in public life: voting, running for office, joining a party or civic group, helping a campaign, contacting officials, supporting or opposing a policy, writing to a newspaper. Name two.

stem_en: What is one way Americans can serve their country?
options_en: Pay a fee to the government
acceptable_en: Work for local, state, or federal government
explanation_en: Americans serve their country by voting, paying taxes, obeying the law, serving in the military, running for office or working in government. Any one is a full answer.

stem_en: Why is it important to pay federal taxes?
options_en: To earn the right to vote
acceptable_en: All people pay to fund the federal government
explanation_en: Paying federal taxes is required by law and by the Constitution (the 16th Amendment); it is how all people fund the federal government, and it is a civic duty.

stem_en: It is important for all men age 18 through 25 to register for the Selective Service. Name one reason why.
options_en: Required to get a driver’s license
acceptable_en: Makes the draft fair, if needed
explanation_en: Men aged 18 through 25 must register for the Selective Service. It is required by law, it is a civic duty, and it keeps a draft fair if one is ever needed.

stem_en: There are four amendments to the Constitution about who can vote. Describe one of them.
acceptable_en: You don’t have to pay (a poll tax) to vote.
Any citizen can vote. (Women and men can vote.)
A male citizen of any race (can vote).
explanation_en: Four amendments widened the vote: the 15th (any race), the 19th (women), the 24th (no poll tax) and the 26th (age 18). Describe any one.

stem_en: What is one responsibility that is only for United States citizens?
explanation_en: Serving on a jury and voting in a federal election are responsibilities only citizens have. Paying taxes and obeying the law apply to everyone.

stem_en: Name one right only for United States citizens.
explanation_en: Voting in a federal election and running for federal office are rights only citizens have. Freedoms of speech and religion belong to everyone in the country.

stem_en: What are two rights of everyone living in the United States?
explanation_en: Everyone living in the United States has freedom of expression, speech, assembly, petition and religion, and the right to bear arms. Name any two.

stem_en: What do we show loyalty to when we say the Pledge of Allegiance?
explanation_en: The Pledge of Allegiance is a promise of loyalty to the flag and to the United States — “the republic for which it stands.”

stem_en: What is one promise you make when you become a United States citizen?
options_en: give up loyalty to other countries
buy a home in the United States
acceptable_en: give up loyalty to other countries
defend the Constitution and laws of the United States
obey the laws of the United States
serve in the U.S. military (if needed)
serve (do important work for) the nation (if needed)
be loyal to the United States
explanation_en: The Oath of Allegiance includes giving up loyalty to other countries, defending the Constitution and laws, obeying U.S. laws, serving in the military or the nation if needed, and being loyal to the United States.

stem_en: How old do citizens have to be to vote for President?
explanation_en: Citizens must be 18 or older to vote for President. The 26th Amendment (1971) lowered the age from 21.

stem_en: What are two ways that Americans can participate in their democracy?
acceptable_en: give an elected official your opinion on an issue
publicly support or oppose an issue or policy
explanation_en: Americans take part in democracy by voting, joining a party or civic group, helping a campaign, contacting their senators and representatives, taking a public stand on an issue, running for office or writing to a newspaper. Name two.

stem_en: When is the last day you can send in federal income tax forms?
explanation_en: Federal income tax returns are due on April 15 each year (or the next business day if that falls on a weekend or holiday).

stem_en: When must all men register for the Selective Service?
explanation_en: All men must register for the Selective Service at age 18 — the window runs from 18 to 26. It is required by law whether or not a draft is ever held.

stem_en: The colonists came to America for many reasons. Name one.
explanation_en: Colonists came for freedom: political liberty, religious freedom, economic opportunity, and to escape persecution at home. Any one is a full answer.

stem_en: Who lived in America before the Europeans arrived?
explanation_en: American Indians — Native Americans — lived across the continent for thousands of years before Europeans arrived.

stem_en: What group of people was taken and sold as slaves?
explanation_en: Africans were taken from Africa and sold as slaves in the American colonies, beginning in the 1600s. Slavery ended with the Civil War and the 13th Amendment.

stem_en: What war did the Americans fight to win independence from Britain?
explanation_en: The American Revolution — the Revolutionary War, or War for Independence — was fought from 1775 to 1783 and won the colonies their independence from Britain.

stem_en: Name one reason why the Americans declared independence from Britain.
options_en: The colonists wanted a king of their own
The British refused to trade with the colonies
acceptable_en: British soldiers stayed in Americans’ houses (boarding, quartering)
explanation_en: The colonists objected to taxation without representation, to British soldiers quartered in their homes, and to having no self-government. The Stamp, Sugar, Townshend and Intolerable Acts, the Boston Massacre and the Boston Tea Party all pushed them toward independence.

stem_en: Who wrote the Declaration of Independence?
explanation_en: Thomas Jefferson wrote the Declaration of Independence in 1776. He later became the third president.

stem_en: When was the Declaration of Independence adopted?
explanation_en: The Declaration of Independence was adopted on July 4, 1776 — the date celebrated every year as Independence Day.

stem_en: The American Revolution had many important events. Name one.
acceptable_en: Washington Crossing the Delaware (Battle of Trenton)
explanation_en: Key events of the Revolution: the Battle of Bunker Hill, the Declaration of Independence, Washington crossing the Delaware (Trenton), the Battle of Saratoga, the winter at Valley Forge, and the British surrender at Yorktown.

stem_en: There were 13 original states. Name five.
explanation_en: The 13 original states: New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecticut, New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Delaware, Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina and Georgia. Name five for the oral test.

stem_en: What founding document was written in 1787?
explanation_en: The Constitution was written at the Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia in 1787. It replaced the Articles of Confederation and took effect in 1789.

stem_en: The Federalist Papers supported the passage of the U.S. Constitution. Name one of the writers.
explanation_en: James Madison, Alexander Hamilton and John Jay wrote the Federalist Papers under the shared pen name Publius, arguing for ratification of the Constitution.

stem_en: Why were the Federalist Papers important?
options_en: They helped people understand the (U.S.) Constitution.
acceptable_en: They helped people understand the (U.S.) Constitution.
explanation_en: The 85 Federalist Papers explained the new Constitution to the public and argued for its ratification; they remain the most important guide to what the framers intended.

stem_en: Benjamin Franklin is famous for many things. Name one.
options_en: Founded the first free public libraries
Third president of the United States
acceptable_en: Founded the first free public libraries
First Postmaster General of the United States
Helped write the Declaration of Independence
explanation_en: Benjamin Franklin founded the first free public libraries, was the first Postmaster General, helped write the Declaration of Independence, invented the lightning rod and bifocals, and served as a diplomat in France.

stem_en: George Washington is famous for many things. Name one.
options_en: Third president of the United States
acceptable_en: First president of the United States
explanation_en: George Washington led the Continental Army, presided over the Constitutional Convention and became the first president — which is why he is called the “Father of Our Country.”

stem_en: Thomas Jefferson is famous for many things. Name one.
options_en: Writer of the Declaration of Independence
First president of the United States
acceptable_en: Writer of the Declaration of Independence
Third president of the United States
Doubled the size of the United States (Louisiana Purchase)
Writer of the Virginia Statute on Religious Freedom
explanation_en: Thomas Jefferson wrote the Declaration of Independence, served as the first Secretary of State and the third president, doubled the country’s size with the Louisiana Purchase, founded the University of Virginia and wrote Virginia’s Statute on Religious Freedom.

stem_en: James Madison is famous for many things. Name one.
options_en: Writer of the Declaration of Independence
acceptable_en: Fourth president of the United States
One of the writers of the Federalist Papers
explanation_en: James Madison is the “Father of the Constitution”: he shaped it at the 1787 convention and co-wrote the Federalist Papers. He was the fourth president and led the country through the War of 1812.

stem_en: Alexander Hamilton is famous for many things. Name one.
options_en: Writer of the Declaration of Independence
Third president of the United States
acceptable_en: One of the writers of the Federalist Papers
Helped establish the First Bank of the United States
explanation_en: Alexander Hamilton was the first Secretary of the Treasury, a writer of the Federalist Papers, founder of the First Bank of the United States, an aide to General Washington and a member of the Continental Congress.

stem_en: What is one reason colonists came to America?
explanation_en: Colonists came for freedom — political liberty, religious freedom, economic opportunity, to practice their religion and to escape persecution.

stem_en: Who lived in America before the Europeans arrived?
explanation_en: American Indians — Native Americans — lived across the continent for thousands of years before Europeans arrived.

stem_en: What group of people was taken to America and sold as slaves?
explanation_en: Africans were taken from Africa and sold as slaves in the colonies, beginning in the 1600s.

stem_en: Why did the colonists fight the British?
options_en: because they wanted a king of their own
because the British refused to trade with them
because of high taxes (taxation without representation)
acceptable_en: because of high taxes (taxation without representation)
because the British army stayed in their houses (boarding, quartering)
explanation_en: The colonists fought because of high taxes imposed without representation in Parliament, because British soldiers were quartered in their homes, and because they had no self-government.

stem_en: Who wrote the Declaration of Independence?
explanation_en: Thomas Jefferson wrote the Declaration of Independence in 1776. He later became the third president.

stem_en: When was the Declaration of Independence adopted?
explanation_en: The Declaration of Independence was adopted on July 4, 1776 — the date celebrated every year as Independence Day.

stem_en: There were 13 original states. Name three.
explanation_en: The 13 original states: New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecticut, New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Delaware, Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina and Georgia. Name three.

stem_en: What happened at the Constitutional Convention?
options_en: The Bill of Rights was ratified.
The colonies declared war on Britain.
The Declaration of Independence was signed.
acceptable_en: The Founding Fathers wrote the Constitution.
explanation_en: At the Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia in 1787, the Founding Fathers wrote the Constitution.

stem_en: When was the Constitution written?
explanation_en: The Constitution was written in 1787 at the Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia and took effect in 1789.

stem_en: The Federalist Papers supported the passage of the U.S. Constitution. Name one of the writers.
explanation_en: James Madison, Alexander Hamilton and John Jay wrote the Federalist Papers under the shared pen name Publius, arguing for ratification of the Constitution.

stem_en: What is one thing Benjamin Franklin is famous for?
options_en: third president of the United States
acceptable_en: oldest member of the Constitutional Convention
first Postmaster General of the United States
explanation_en: Benjamin Franklin was a U.S. diplomat, the oldest member of the Constitutional Convention, the first Postmaster General, the writer of “Poor Richard’s Almanac,” and he started the first free libraries.

stem_en: Who is the “Father of Our Country”?
explanation_en: George Washington is the “Father of Our Country”: commander of the Continental Army, president of the Constitutional Convention and the first president.

stem_en: Who was the first President?
explanation_en: George Washington was the first President of the United States, serving from 1789 to 1797.

stem_en: What territory did the United States buy from France in 1803?
explanation_en: In 1803 the United States bought the Louisiana Territory from France for about $15 million, doubling the country’s size. Jefferson was president.

stem_en: Name one war fought by the United States in the 1800s.
explanation_en: The United States fought four wars in the 1800s: the War of 1812, the Mexican-American War (1846–48), the Civil War (1861–65) and the Spanish-American War (1898).

stem_en: Name the U.S. war between the North and the South.
explanation_en: The Civil War (1861–1865) was fought between the North (the Union) and the South (the Confederacy). It is also called the War between the States.

stem_en: The Civil War had many important events. Name one.
explanation_en: Key Civil War events: Fort Sumter (the first shots), Antietam, the Emancipation Proclamation, Vicksburg, Gettysburg, Sherman’s March, the surrender at Appomattox, and Lincoln’s assassination.

stem_en: Abraham Lincoln is famous for many things. Name one.
options_en: First president of the United States
acceptable_en: Led the United States during the Civil War
explanation_en: Abraham Lincoln, the 16th president, led the United States through the Civil War, saved the Union, freed the slaves with the Emancipation Proclamation and delivered the Gettysburg Address.

stem_en: What did the Emancipation Proclamation do?
options_en: Admitted new states to the Union
Gave women the right to vote
acceptable_en: Freed slaves in the Confederate states
Freed slaves in most Southern states
explanation_en: The Emancipation Proclamation (1863) freed the slaves in the Confederate states — most of the South. Slavery everywhere ended with the 13th Amendment in 1865.

stem_en: What U.S. war ended slavery?
explanation_en: The Civil War ended slavery: the Emancipation Proclamation came during the war, and the 13th Amendment, ratified in 1865, abolished it everywhere.

stem_en: What amendment says all persons born or naturalized in the United States, and subject to the jurisdiction thereof, are U.S. citizens?
explanation_en: The 14th Amendment (1868) says that everyone born or naturalized in the United States is a citizen, and guarantees equal protection of the laws.

stem_en: When did all men get the right to vote?
explanation_en: The 15th Amendment, ratified in 1870 during Reconstruction after the Civil War, said the right to vote could not be denied because of race — so all men could vote.

stem_en: Name one leader of the women’s rights movement in the 1800s.
explanation_en: Leaders of the 1800s women’s rights movement included Susan B. Anthony, Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Sojourner Truth, Harriet Tubman, Lucretia Mott and Lucy Stone.

stem_en: What territory did the United States buy from France in 1803?
explanation_en: In 1803 the United States bought the Louisiana Territory from France for about $15 million, doubling the country’s size. Jefferson was president.

stem_en: Name one war fought by the United States in the 1800s.
explanation_en: The United States fought four wars in the 1800s: the War of 1812, the Mexican-American War (1846–48), the Civil War (1861–65) and the Spanish-American War (1898).

stem_en: Name the U.S. war between the North and the South.
explanation_en: The Civil War (1861–1865) was fought between the North (the Union) and the South (the Confederacy). It is also called the War between the States.

stem_en: Name one problem that led to the Civil War.
explanation_en: Slavery, economic differences between North and South, and disputes over states’ rights led to the Civil War.

stem_en: What was one important thing that Abraham Lincoln did?
acceptable_en: led the United States during the Civil War
explanation_en: Lincoln freed the slaves with the Emancipation Proclamation, saved the Union and led the country through the Civil War.

stem_en: What did the Emancipation Proclamation do?
options_en: Admitted new states to the Union
Gave women the right to vote
acceptable_en: freed slaves in the Confederate states
freed slaves in most Southern states
explanation_en: The Emancipation Proclamation (1863) freed the slaves in the Confederate states — most of the South. Slavery everywhere ended with the 13th Amendment in 1865.

stem_en: What did Susan B. Anthony do?
explanation_en: Susan B. Anthony fought for women’s rights, above all the right to vote, and for civil rights. The 19th Amendment is sometimes called the Susan B. Anthony Amendment.

stem_en: Name one war fought by the United States in the 1900s.
explanation_en: In the 1900s the United States fought World War I, World War II, the Korean War, the Vietnam War and the Persian Gulf War.

stem_en: Why did the United States enter World War I?
options_en: To force the Iraqi military from Kuwait
To stop the spread of communism
acceptable_en: To support the Allied Powers (England, France, Italy, and Russia)
To oppose the Central Powers (Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire, and Bulgaria)
explanation_en: The United States entered World War I in 1917 after Germany attacked American civilian ships, joining the Allied Powers against Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria.

stem_en: When did all women get the right to vote?
explanation_en: Women won the right to vote in 1920, after World War I, with the 19th Amendment.

stem_en: What was the Great Depression?
options_en: A war between the North and the South
Longest economic recession in modern history
acceptable_en: Longest economic recession in modern history
explanation_en: The Great Depression, which began with the stock market crash of 1929, was the longest and deepest economic recession in modern history, lasting through the 1930s.

stem_en: When did the Great Depression start?
explanation_en: The Great Depression began with the Great Crash — the stock market crash of October 1929.

stem_en: Who was president during the Great Depression and World War II?
explanation_en: Franklin D. Roosevelt was president from 1933 to 1945, through the Great Depression and most of World War II. He is the only president elected four times.

stem_en: Why did the United States enter World War II?
options_en: To stop the spread of communism
acceptable_en: To support the Allied Powers (England, France, and Russia)
To oppose the Axis Powers (Germany, Italy, and Japan)
explanation_en: The United States entered World War II after Japan bombed Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941, joining the Allies against the Axis Powers — Germany, Italy and Japan.

stem_en: Dwight Eisenhower is famous for many things. Name one.
acceptable_en: President at the end of (during) the Korean War
Signed the Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956 (Created the Interstate System)
explanation_en: Dwight Eisenhower commanded Allied forces in Europe in World War II, was the 34th president, ended the Korean War and created the Interstate Highway System in 1956.

stem_en: Who was the United States’ main rival during the Cold War?
explanation_en: During the Cold War (roughly 1947–1991) the United States’ main rival was the Soviet Union (the USSR), of which Russia was the largest part.

stem_en: During the Cold War, what was one main concern of the United States?
explanation_en: During the Cold War the United States’ main concerns were the spread of communism and the threat of nuclear war with the Soviet Union.

stem_en: Why did the United States enter the Korean War?
options_en: To force the Iraqi military from Kuwait
To stop the spread of communism
acceptable_en: To stop the spread of communism
explanation_en: The United States entered the Korean War (1950–53) to stop the spread of communism after communist North Korea invaded South Korea.

stem_en: Why did the United States enter the Vietnam War?
options_en: To stop the spread of communism
To force the Iraqi military from Kuwait
acceptable_en: To stop the spread of communism
explanation_en: The United States fought in Vietnam to stop the spread of communism from North Vietnam to the South.

stem_en: What did the civil rights movement do?
options_en: Fought to end the Vietnam War
Won women the right to vote
explanation_en: The civil rights movement of the 1950s and 1960s fought to end racial discrimination, winning the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

stem_en: Martin Luther King, Jr. is famous for many things. Name one.
acceptable_en: Worked for equality for all Americans
Worked to ensure that people would “not be judged by the color of their skin, but by the content of their character”
explanation_en: Martin Luther King, Jr. led the civil rights movement, working for equality for all Americans and for a nation where people are judged “not by the color of their skin, but by the content of their character.”

stem_en: Why did the United States enter the Persian Gulf War?
options_en: To force the Iraqi military from Kuwait
To stop the spread of communism
acceptable_en: To force the Iraqi military from Kuwait
explanation_en: In the Persian Gulf War (1991) the United States led a coalition to force the Iraqi military out of Kuwait, which Iraq had invaded.

stem_en: What major event happened on September 11, 2001 in the United States?
acceptable_en: Terrorists took over two planes and crashed them into the World Trade Center in New York City
Terrorists took over a plane and crashed into the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia
Terrorists took over a plane originally aimed at Washington, D.C., and crashed in a field in Pennsylvania
explanation_en: On September 11, 2001, terrorists hijacked four planes, crashing two into the World Trade Center in New York, one into the Pentagon, and one — aimed at Washington — into a field in Pennsylvania.

stem_en: Name one U.S. military conflict after the September 11, 2001 attacks.
explanation_en: After the September 11 attacks the United States began the War on Terror, including the war in Afghanistan (2001) and the war in Iraq (2003).

stem_en: Name one American Indian tribe in the United States.
note_en: For a complete list of tribes, please visit bia.gov.
explanation_en: USCIS lists many federally recognized tribes, among them the Apache, Cherokee, Cheyenne, Chippewa, Choctaw, Creek, Hopi, Lakota, Mohawk, Navajo, Pueblo, Seminole, Seneca, Sioux and Shawnee. Any one is a full answer.

stem_en: Name one example of an American innovation.
explanation_en: American innovations include the light bulb, the automobile and assembly line, skyscrapers, the airplane, the integrated circuit and landing on the moon.

stem_en: Name one war fought by the United States in the 1900s.
explanation_en: In the 1900s the United States fought World War I, World War II, the Korean War, the Vietnam War and the Persian Gulf War.

stem_en: Who was President during World War I?
explanation_en: Woodrow Wilson was president during World War I (1913–1921).

stem_en: Who was President during the Great Depression and World War II?
explanation_en: Franklin D. Roosevelt was president from 1933 to 1945, through the Great Depression and most of World War II. He is the only president elected four times.

stem_en: Who did the United States fight in World War II?
explanation_en: In World War II the United States fought the Axis Powers: Japan, Germany and Italy.

stem_en: Before he was President, Eisenhower was a general. What war was he in?
explanation_en: Eisenhower was the Supreme Allied Commander in Europe during World War II before becoming president in 1953.

stem_en: During the Cold War, what was the main concern of the United States?
explanation_en: During the Cold War the United States’ main concern was communism and its spread from the Soviet Union.

stem_en: What movement tried to end racial discrimination?
explanation_en: The civil rights movement of the 1950s and 1960s tried to end racial discrimination, winning the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

stem_en: What did Martin Luther King, Jr. do?
acceptable_en: worked for equality for all Americans
explanation_en: Martin Luther King, Jr. fought for civil rights and worked for equality for all Americans, leading the movement until his assassination in 1968.

stem_en: What major event happened on September 11, 2001, in the United States?
explanation_en: On September 11, 2001, terrorists hijacked four planes, crashing two into the World Trade Center in New York, one into the Pentagon, and one — aimed at Washington — into a field in Pennsylvania.

stem_en: Name one American Indian tribe in the United States.
note_en: USCIS Officers will be supplied with a list of federally recognized American Indian tribes.
explanation_en: USCIS lists many federally recognized tribes, among them the Apache, Cherokee, Cheyenne, Chippewa, Choctaw, Creek, Hopi, Lakota, Mohawk, Navajo, Pueblo, Seminole, Seneca, Sioux and Shawnee. Any one is a full answer.

stem_en: Name one of the two longest rivers in the United States.
explanation_en: The Missouri and the Mississippi are the two longest rivers in the United States; they meet near St. Louis.

stem_en: What ocean is on the West Coast of the United States?
explanation_en: The Pacific Ocean lies off the West Coast — California, Oregon, Washington, Alaska and Hawaii.

stem_en: What ocean is on the East Coast of the United States?
explanation_en: The Atlantic Ocean lies off the East Coast, from Maine to Florida.

stem_en: Name one U.S. territory.
explanation_en: The U.S. territories are Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, American Samoa, the Northern Mariana Islands and Guam. Hawaii and Alaska are states.

stem_en: Name one state that borders Canada.
explanation_en: Thirteen states border Canada: Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont, New York, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Michigan, Minnesota, North Dakota, Montana, Idaho, Washington and Alaska.

stem_en: Name one state that borders Mexico.
explanation_en: Four states border Mexico: California, Arizona, New Mexico and Texas.

stem_en: What is the capital of the United States?
explanation_en: Washington, D.C. has been the capital since 1800. The District of Columbia is not part of any state.

stem_en: Where is the Statue of Liberty?
note_en: Also acceptable are New Jersey, near New York City, and on the Hudson (River).
explanation_en: The Statue of Liberty stands on Liberty Island in New York Harbor. It was a gift from France in 1886.

stem_en: What is the capital of the United States?
explanation_en: Washington, D.C. has been the capital since 1800. The District of Columbia is not part of any state.

stem_en: Where is the Statue of Liberty?
note_en: Also acceptable are New Jersey, near New York City, and on the Hudson (River).
explanation_en: The Statue of Liberty stands on Liberty Island in New York Harbor. It was a gift from France in 1886.

stem_en: Why does the flag have 13 stripes?
acceptable_en: (Because the stripes) represent the original colonies
explanation_en: The flag’s 13 stripes stand for the 13 original colonies that became the first states.

stem_en: Why does the flag have 50 stars?
options_en: (Because there is) one star for each state
One for each year of the Revolution
acceptable_en: (Because there is) one star for each state
explanation_en: The flag has 50 stars because there are 50 states — one star for each. The 50th star was added for Hawaii in 1960.

stem_en: What is the name of the national anthem?
explanation_en: The national anthem is “The Star-Spangled Banner,” written by Francis Scott Key during the War of 1812 and adopted officially in 1931.

stem_en: The Nation’s first motto was “E Pluribus Unum.” What does that mean?
explanation_en: “E Pluribus Unum” is Latin for “Out of many, one”: many states and many peoples forming one nation. It appears on the Great Seal and on U.S. coins.

stem_en: Why does the flag have 13 stripes?
acceptable_en: because the stripes represent the original colonies
explanation_en: The flag’s 13 stripes stand for the 13 original colonies that became the first states.

stem_en: Why does the flag have 50 stars?
options_en: One for each year of the Revolution
because there is one star for each state
acceptable_en: because there is one star for each state
because each star represents a state
explanation_en: The flag has 50 stars because there are 50 states — one star for each. The 50th star was added for Hawaii in 1960.

stem_en: What is the name of the national anthem?
explanation_en: The national anthem is “The Star-Spangled Banner,” written by Francis Scott Key during the War of 1812 and adopted officially in 1931.

stem_en: What is Independence Day?
options_en: A holiday to honor American workers
A holiday to celebrate U.S. independence (from Britain)
A holiday to honor soldiers who died in military service
The first day of the year
acceptable_en: A holiday to celebrate U.S. independence (from Britain)
explanation_en: Independence Day, July 4, celebrates the adoption of the Declaration of Independence in 1776 — the country’s birthday.

stem_en: Name three national U.S. holidays.
explanation_en: The eleven national holidays: New Year’s Day, Martin Luther King, Jr. Day, Presidents Day, Memorial Day, Juneteenth, Independence Day, Labor Day, Columbus Day, Veterans Day, Thanksgiving and Christmas. Name three.

stem_en: What is Memorial Day?
options_en: A holiday to celebrate U.S. independence
A holiday to honor American workers
A holiday to honor people in the military
A holiday to honor soldiers who died in military service
acceptable_en: A holiday to honor soldiers who died in military service
explanation_en: Memorial Day, the last Monday in May, honors soldiers who died in military service. Veterans Day honors everyone who has served.

stem_en: What is Veterans Day?
options_en: A holiday to honor soldiers who died in military service
A holiday to honor American workers
A holiday to honor people in the (U.S.) military
A holiday to celebrate U.S. independence
acceptable_en: A holiday to honor people in the (U.S.) military
A holiday to honor people who have served (in the U.S. military)
explanation_en: Veterans Day, November 11, honors everyone who has served in the U.S. military. Memorial Day honors those who died in service.

stem_en: When do we celebrate Independence Day?
explanation_en: Independence Day is celebrated on July 4, the date the Declaration of Independence was adopted in 1776.

stem_en: Name two national U.S. holidays.
explanation_en: National holidays include New Year’s Day, Martin Luther King, Jr. Day, Presidents’ Day, Memorial Day, Independence Day, Labor Day, Columbus Day, Veterans Day, Thanksgiving and Christmas. Name two.
